paragraphs: There are three kinds of tallit. The first is made of the wool of ewes and rams, and in this tallit the tzitzit are also made from the aforementioned wool. This is the obligation from the Torah according to all opinions, and one who wears it fulfills a positive commandment from the Torah according to all opinions.

The second is a tallit of cotton or a tallit of silk. Regarding this there is a dispute: some say the obligation is from the Torah, and some say the obligation is only from the Rabbis - and even according to the opinion that the obligation is rabbinic, one may still recite a blessing over it, just as one recites a blessing over a rabbinic commandment. Regarding the tzitzit: although according to Maran (the Shulchan Aruch) of blessed memory and those who agree with him, one may place tzitzit of ewes' wool even on garments of other materials, nevertheless if the tallit is of cotton it is good to place on it tzitzit of its own kind, namely cotton, because according to the Maharam of Rothenburg of blessed memory and those who agree with him, tzitzit of wool do not exempt garments of other materials. Therefore, in order to satisfy both sides of the aforementioned dispute, one should place tzitzit of the garment's own material - but this is specifically where the tallit is cotton, in which case one places cotton tzitzit. However, if the tallit is of silk, it is difficult to find silk tzitzit properly prepared for their designated purpose according to all opinions, because one great authority, cited by the "Birkei Yosef" of blessed memory, siman 102, holds that with silk the throwing and drawing of the thread must be done for the sake of the mitzvah, since the throwing and drawing in silk is like spinning in wool - see there. Accordingly it is difficult to find silk tzitzit properly prepared according to this view, and even though the "Terumat HaDeshen" of blessed memory appears not to hold like that aforementioned authority, nevertheless there is a genuine dispute, and perhaps even Maran of blessed memory holds like that authority. Therefore, for a silk tallit, if one cannot find silk tzitzit properly prepared according to the view of that aforementioned authority, one should place on this silk tallit threads of ewes' wool instead. You thus find that a silk tallit, aside from being only rabbinically obligated, is even worse than a cotton tallit because of the need to hang wool threads on it that are not of its own material, and in all these cases there is a further deficiency compared to a tallit of ewes' wool, in that there the obligation is according to all opinions, whereas here there is the view of the Baal HaIttur and the Bach of blessed memory who hold that one should not recite a blessing except over a tallit of ewes' wool with woolen threads, and that over a tallit of other materials one should not recite a blessing at all - though we do not rule according to them in this matter.

The third is a tallit whose warp is of ewes' wool and whose weft is of another material, or vice versa, and this is the worst of all, since according to the Maharam and those who agree with him there is no remedy for this tallit as regards the threads, and only according to Maran of blessed memory does it have a remedy, by hanging on it threads of ewes' wool, and so one must do. Therefore it is fitting for every one who fears Heaven to be careful, both with a large tallit and with a small tallit, to wear one of ewes' wool, and let the threads likewise be of ewes' wool, and thereby he fulfills the positive commandment from the Torah and discharges his obligation regarding tzitzit according to all opinions without any doubt.

clarification.explanation: There are three types of tallit. The first - a tallit of the wool of ewes (females) or rams (males), whose tzitzit are also made from that same wool. This is the obligation from the Torah according to everyone, and whoever wears it certainly fulfills a positive commandment from the Torah. The second - a tallit of cotton or silk, regarding which there is a dispute: some say the obligation is from the Torah, and some say the obligation is only rabbinic - but even according to this latter view one may recite a blessing over it. Regarding the tzitzit: although according to Maran (the Shulchan Aruch) it is permitted to use woolen tzitzit even on a garment of another material, it is nevertheless preferable that a cotton tallit have tzitzit of the same material, because some hold (following the Maharam of Rothenburg) that woolen tzitzit do not exempt a garment of a different material. But for a silk tallit it is difficult to find valid silk tzitzit according to all views, because one authority held that silk requires a special spinning process performed for the sake of the mitzvah, and therefore a silk tallit should specifically use tzitzit of ewes' wool. It follows that a silk tallit, besides being only rabbinically obligated, is even worse than a cotton tallit in that it needs tzitzit of a different material - and there is even an opinion (the Baal HaIttur and the Bach) that one should not recite a blessing at all over a tallit that is not of ewes' wool - though the halachah does not follow this opinion. The third type - a tallit whose warp is of ewes' wool and whose weft is of another material (or vice versa), and this is the worst of all, for according to the Maharam there is no remedy for this tallit regarding its threads, and only according to Maran is there a remedy, by hanging threads of ewes' wool on it - and so one must do: whoever has such a tallit should hang threads of ewes' wool on it. Therefore, one who fears Heaven should always take care - both with a large tallit and with a small tallit - to wear only a tallit of ewes' wool, with tzitzit threads also of ewes' wool, and thereby fulfill the mitzvah according to everyone without any doubt.
takeaways: The most excellent tallit, obligatory from the Torah according to everyone, is made from the wool of ewes or rams, with tzitzit of that same wool.

Cotton or silk tallitot are disputed as to whether their obligation is from the Torah or only rabbinic, and it is nevertheless preferable to use tzitzit of the same material (except for silk, where it is hard to find valid tzitzit, so wool is used instead).

The worst case is a tallit whose warp and weft are of different materials - one who has such a tallit must hang threads of ewes' wool on it; and ideally, everyone's choice should be a tallit and tzitzit of ewes' wool alone.

paragraphs: There are kinds of garments called "karman," and also what are called "shaal keshmir," which are made from goat hair, called in the holy tongue "the plumage of goats." These have the same status as other materials such as cotton, silk, or hemp, because throughout the Torah, "wool" unqualified refers only to the wool of ewes, which are the females, or the wool of rams, which are the males; but that of goats is called "the plumage of goats." Therefore one who fears Heaven should investigate the tallitot he purchases, since some appear to be of ewes' and rams' wool, but in truth are of camel hair or goat hair, and some have the warp of wool and the weft of another material - these are even worse, as stated above.

clarification.explanation: There are types of garments called "karman" and "shaal keshmir," made from goat hair (called in the holy tongue "the plumage of goats"). Their status is the same as other non-kosher-wool fabrics, such as cotton, silk, or hemp - because throughout the Torah, unqualified "wool" refers only to the wool of ewes or rams, whereas goat hair is called by a different name. Therefore, one who fears Heaven must carefully examine the tallitot he buys, since sometimes they appear to be ewes' wool but are actually camel or goat hair, or the warp is one kind and the weft another - and such a tallit is even worse, as explained previously.
takeaways: Goat hair (or camel hair) is not considered "wool" for the purpose of the tallit, and has the same status as other materials that are not obligatory from the Torah.
One must carefully check that a tallit being purchased is truly made of ewes' or rams' wool, and not a similar-looking material that is actually goat or camel hair.

paragraphs: A garment made of leather is exempt according to all opinions, since only a woven item is called a "garment" for the obligation of tzitzit.

clarification.explanation: A garment made of leather is entirely exempt from tzitzit according to everyone, since only something that is woven is called a "garment" for the purpose of the tzitzit obligation - and leather is not woven.
takeaways: A leather garment is exempt from tzitzit, because the tzitzit obligation applies only to a woven garment.

paragraphs: Although linen threads exempt a garment of other materials, it is forbidden to hang them on a woolen garment because of shatnez (forbidden mixture), since the Torah permitted the mixture in tzitzit only where there is techelet, and in our time we have no techelet. Some say, however, that one should not hang linen threads even on a garment of other materials that are not wool, lest there be a wool that looks like silk, and one come to place linen tzitzit on a woolen garment thinking it is silk. Accordingly, the practice is not to place linen threads on garments of any kind other than wool.

clarification.explanation: Linen threads exempt in principle a garment of another material (that is, they may be placed on a garment that is not wool), but it is forbidden to place them on a woolen garment, because of the prohibition of shatnez - since the Torah permitted the mixture in tzitzit only when there is a thread of techelet, and in our time we have no techelet. Some even hold that linen threads should not be placed even on a garment of another material that is not wool, out of concern that there are types of wool that resemble silk in appearance, and someone might mistakenly think it is a silk garment rather than wool, and mistakenly place linen on wool. Therefore the prevailing custom is not to place linen threads at all on any garment.
takeaways: It is forbidden to place linen tzitzit threads on a woolen garment, due to the prohibition of shatnez, as long as there is no techelet.
The prevailing custom is to avoid linen threads altogether, even on a non-woolen garment, out of concern for confusing the types of fabric.

paragraphs: One should not wear a linen tallit at all, even if linen threads are hung on it, as a preventive decree. Only in a case of great necessity, when one has no other garment besides linen, should one hang specifically linen threads on it, and not another kind - and this leniency was granted only in such a pressing situation where one has no other tallit.

clarification.explanation: One should not wear a linen tallit at all, even with linen threads hung on it (as required), because of a preventive decree. Only in a case of great necessity, when one has no garment other than linen, should one hang specifically linen threads on it (and no other kind), and this leniency applies only in a pressing situation where there is no other tallit available.
takeaways: One should not wear a linen tallit at all, except in a case of great necessity when there is no other option - and then one should specifically hang linen threads on it.

paragraphs: A tallit that does not have four corners is exempt from tzitzit, and if it has five corners or more it is obligated - but one should hang tzitzit only on four of its corners, not on all of them, and one must take care to place the threads on the four corners that are most distant from one another, since the more distant ones bear the name "corner" more properly. If one transgressed and hung tzitzit on more than four corners, he transgresses the prohibition of "bal tosif" (do not add) when he wears it. In any case, one should take care to keep away from such a tallit altogether and not wear a tallit with more than four corners, even if tzitzit are hung on only four of them, because there are those who dispute this and exempt such a tallit entirely from tzitzit, as mentioned by the halachic authorities.

clarification.explanation: A tallit that does not have four corners is exempt from the mitzvah, and if it has five corners or more it is obligated - but tzitzit should be hung on only four of them, not on all. One must take care to place the threads on the four corners most distant from one another, since a corner that is more distant is considered more properly a "corner" in the halachic sense. Whoever hangs tzitzit on more than four corners transgresses the prohibition of "bal tosif" when wearing it. In any case, it is proper to avoid from the outset wearing a tallit with more than four corners, even if threads are hung on only four of them, because there are those who dispute this and hold that such a tallit is entirely exempt from the mitzvah.
takeaways: A tallit with fewer than four corners is exempt; with five or more it is obligated, but tzitzit should be hung only on the four most distant corners.
Hanging tzitzit on more than four corners is forbidden as "bal tosif," so it is best from the outset not to wear a tallit with more than four corners.

paragraphs: The corners of the tallit - the edges on which tzitzit are hung - must be specifically square and not round, since a rounded shape is not called a "corner." One must be especially careful about this with a tallit katan, because of the stitching done on them, which can easily make them appear rounded due to the seam.

clarification.explanation: The corners of the tallit on which the tzitzit are hung must be specifically square, not round, because a round shape is not considered a "corner" halachically. One must be especially careful about this with a tallit katan, since due to the stitching process involved, the corners can easily appear rounded without one noticing.
takeaways: The corners of the tallit on which tzitzit are hung must be square; one must be especially careful with a tallit katan that the stitching does not inadvertently round them.

paragraphs: If one's tallit tears, he should take care to sew it immediately so that it does not end up with six corners, since there is an opinion that holds it would then be exempt from tzitzit, as I wrote above. And if most of it tears and one comes to sew it, one must untie the tzitzit and re-hang them after the sewing - so the later authorities have ruled, the reason being "you shall make" and not from something already made, according to the opinion that exempts it in this case. Although we do not rule according to this opinion, since Maran of blessed memory ruled that it remains obligated, nevertheless one should be careful about this from the outset. This situation is common with a large tallit made from two pieces of cloth sewn together, where sometimes the stitching threads wear out and the pieces come apart from each other.

clarification.explanation: If a tallit tears, one should take care to sew it immediately so that it does not remain with six corners (as a result of the tear), because some hold that a tallit with six corners is exempt from tzitzit, as mentioned earlier. If most of the tallit tears and one wishes to sew it, one must first untie the tzitzit and re-hang them after the sewing - so the later authorities ruled, for the reason of "you shall make it" and not from something already made (the tzitzit must be made on a garment that is already complete and finished), following the opinion that exempts a tallit whose greater part has torn. Although the halachah does not follow this opinion (Maran ruled that the tallit remains obligated), one should nevertheless be careful about this from the outset. This situation is common with a large tallit made of two pieces of cloth sewn together, where sometimes the stitching threads wear out and the fabric comes apart.
takeaways: A torn tallit should be sewn immediately, so that it does not end up with six corners.
If most of the tallit tears, one must untie the tzitzit before sewing and re-hang them afterward, in order to satisfy all opinions.

paragraphs: A scarf placed around the neck is exempt from tzitzit even though it has four corners and is of sufficient size for the obligation. The same law applies to garments such as a cloak and the like, which have two corners at the top near the neck and two corners at the bottom - these are exempt. Nevertheless, one who fears Heaven should take care to make one of the corners rounded, for then it would be exempt according to all opinions, and even though the world has not been accustomed to be concerned about this, one who is stringent will be blessed - see the later authorities there.

clarification.explanation: A scarf worn around the neck is exempt from tzitzit, even if it has four corners and a sufficient measure to be obligated, and the same law applies to garments such as a cloak and the like, which have two corners at the top near the neck and two corners at the bottom - these are exempt. Nevertheless, one who fears Heaven should take care to make one of the corners rounded, and then it would be exempt according to all opinions, even though the world has not been accustomed to be concerned about this.
takeaways: A garment with corners at the top (near the neck) and corners at the bottom, such as a scarf or cloak, is exempt from tzitzit.
One who is stringent and rounds one of the corners, to satisfy all opinions, will be blessed.

paragraphs: It is the most excellent way of performing the mitzvah to make the tzitzit threads spun from eight threads, such that each of the eight threads is itself made of eight strands twisted together, so that the total threads on the four corners would be 256, a hint to the wings of the Chayot (the celestial creatures). This practice is valid, as the "Shiyurei Berachah" of blessed memory wrote in the name of a certain holy sage there, and in the book Lev Chayim, siman 86, several books are cited that write likewise. Therefore everyone should be careful about this from the outset,

clarification.explanation: It is the most excellent way to perform the mitzvah to make the tzitzit threads spun from eight threads, each of the eight itself doubled from eight thinner threads, so that in total there would be two hundred fifty-six (256) threads across the four corners - a hint to the "wings of the Chayot" in the Divine Chariot. This is a valid and recommended practice, as cited by several works of halachah and Kabbalah.
takeaways: It is the most excellent way to make tzitzit threads spun from eight, so that across all four corners there are 256 threads, as a hint to the wings of the Chayot.

paragraphs: And I have found, with the help of Heaven, a further hint in this: the word "muvchar" ("most excellent") itself has the numerical value of 256, meaning that this matter is indeed the most excellent way of the mitzvah - and this is what is written, "Sing joyfully, O Yaakov, with gladness" ("renu l'Yaakov simchah"). And it is known that one must pass these four corners, which total 256 threads, over one's eyes at the time of the recitation of the Shema, and the letters of the word "ayin" (eye), spelled out in full, likewise total 256 - a hint that these threads (which total 256) benefit the eye (whose numerical hint is 256). It further follows that each corner has sixty-four threads, corresponding to the numerical value of "nogah" (radiance) - by virtue of which we rectify the kelipah (husk) of Nogah, and remove the "garment of skin" so that it becomes a "garment of light" from the four worlds, corresponding to the four corners.

clarification.explanation: The Ben Ish Chai adds a hint of his own: the word "muvchar" (most excellent, describing the mitzvah in the previous section) has the numerical value of 256, matching the number of tzitzit threads mentioned. He connects this to the verse "Sing joyfully, O Yaakov, with gladness" ("renu l'Yaakov simchah"), and notes that at the time of reciting the Shema it is customary to pass the four corners (whose threads total 256) over the eyes - and the letters of the word "ayin" (eye), when spelled out in full, likewise total 256, hinting that these threads benefit the eye. He adds further: each corner by itself contains sixty-four (64) threads, corresponding to the numerical value of "nogah" - and by virtue of this one rectifies the kelipah of Nogah, and transforms the "garment of skin" (representing the physical body) into a "garment of light" that shines from the four worlds, corresponding to the four corners.
takeaways: The Ben Ish Chai adds several gematria hints: "muvchar" equals 256 like the number of tzitzit threads, and "ayin" (eye) spelled in full also equals 256 - linking the tzitzit to the rectification of sight.
According to the esoteric tradition, each corner (sixty-four threads, matching the value of "nogah") helps rectify the kelipah of Nogah and transform the "garment of skin" into a "garment of light."

paragraphs: One should take care that the body of the tallit and the tzitzit threads be entirely white, both for a large tallit and for a small tallit, as a hint to the matter, "and those wrapped shall be in white." Tallitot that have a colored stripe on the side for adornment pose no problem, since the color is a very minor part relative to the body of the tallit, most of which is white.

clarification.explanation: One should take care that the body of the tallit and the tzitzit threads be entirely white, both for a large tallit and a small tallit, as a hint to the verse "and those wrapped shall be in white." Tallitot that have a decorative colored stripe on the sides pose no problem, since the color is a small minority relative to the body of the tallit, most of which is white.
takeaways: The body of the tallit and the tzitzit threads should be white; decorative colored stripes on the sides do not detract from this as long as most of the fabric is white.

paragraphs: The four tzitzit threads should be placed through the hole in the corner of the tallit, so that there are eight threads hanging, four on each side, and each of these eight threads must be twelve thumb-widths long, measured at the widest part of the thumb. One begins measuring from the edge of the corner after the knot, but whatever lies upon the corner itself is not included in the count of the twelve thumb-widths. If one wishes to make them longer than twelve thumb-widths, he may do so, and after the fact, if they are less than twelve thumb-widths they are still valid - and all the more so if they originally had the full measure of twelve but shrank somewhat through washing, in which case they are certainly valid after the fact.

clarification.explanation: The four tzitzit threads are inserted through the hole in the corner of the tallit, so that eight threads hang there - four on each side. The length of each of the eight threads should be about twelve thumb-widths, measured at the widest point of the thumb. One measures from the edge of the corner after the knot, but the portion lying on the body of the corner itself is not included within the twelve thumb-widths. It is permitted to lengthen the threads beyond this measure, and after the fact, even threads shorter than twelve thumb-widths are valid - and this applies all the more if they originally had the full measure and only shrank slightly from washing, in which case they remain valid after the fact.
takeaways: The tzitzit threads - eight threads on each corner - should be about twelve thumb-widths long, measured from the edge of the corner after the knot.
After the fact, shorter threads, or ones that shrank from washing, remain valid.

paragraphs: Of these twelve thumb-widths, one should take care to make four thumb-widths the "gedil" (the wound/twisted section) and eight thumb-widths the "anaf" (the loose, free-hanging section), and if one adds to the gedil he should likewise add to the anaf, in such a way that he is careful that the tzitzit always maintain a ratio of one-third gedil and two-thirds anaf, for there is a reason for this according to the esoteric tradition.

clarification.explanation: Of these twelve thumb-widths, one should take care that four thumb-widths be the "gedil" (the wound/twisted section) and eight thumb-widths be the "anaf" (the loose, free-hanging section), so that the ratio is always one-third gedil and two-thirds anaf - and if one lengthens the gedil, he must correspondingly lengthen the anaf as well, to preserve this ratio. There is a reason for this according to the esoteric tradition.
takeaways: The ratio in the tzitzit threads is always one-third "gedil" (twisted) to two-thirds "anaf" (free), and this ratio must be preserved even when the threads are lengthened.

paragraphs: One should tie the ends of each and every tzitzit thread so that they do not come undone from their twisting. So testified our teacher Rabbi Chaim Vital of blessed memory regarding our teacher the Ari of blessed memory, that he used to do so, and so testified our teacher Rabbi Shmuel Vital of blessed memory regarding our teacher Rabbi Chaim Vital, his father, of blessed memory.

clarification.explanation: One should tie the ends of each and every tzitzit thread, so that they do not come undone from their twisting. So Rabbi Chaim Vital testified in the name of his teacher the Arizal, that he used to do this, and so also his son Rabbi Shmuel Vital testified regarding his father Rabbi Chaim Vital.
takeaways: One should tie the ends of the tzitzit threads so that they do not come undone - a practice given authority by the tradition of the Arizal and Rabbi Chaim Vital.

paragraphs: Our teacher Rabbi Chaim Vital of blessed memory testified regarding our teacher the Ari of blessed memory, that he was accustomed, specifically in a tallit katan, to make two holes adjacent to each other, resembling the vowel point "tzeirei," in each of the four corners, and he would draw the tzitzit threads through those two holes, in such a way that the two ends of the tzitzit threads would show on the other, outer side. This view is cited in the book Ha'Agur, but our teacher the Ari of blessed memory did not do this in a large tallit, only in a small tallit. And our teacher Rabbi Shmuel Vital of blessed memory testified regarding his father, our teacher Rabbi Chaim Vital, that he did not do so even in a tallit katan. Certainly our teacher Rabbi Chaim Vital of blessed memory understood from our teacher the Ari of blessed memory that this matter is not indispensable, and that our teacher the Ari of blessed memory, having been accustomed to it in his childhood following the custom of the Ashkenazim, simply did not change it. Therefore our teacher Rabbi Chaim Vital of blessed memory likewise did not change his own custom, whereas our custom is to make a single hole even in a tallit katan. And I have heard that among the Chassidim in Jerusalem, may it be built and established, the simple custom is likewise to make a single hole both in a large tallit and in a small tallit, and presumably such was also the custom of our teacher the Rashash of blessed memory.

clarification.explanation: Rabbi Chaim Vital testified that his teacher the Arizal was accustomed, specifically in a tallit katan, to make two holes adjacent to each other (like the shape of the vowel point "tzeirei") in each of the four corners, drawing the tzitzit threads through these two holes so that the ends of the threads would show on the other, outer side. This approach is also cited in the book Ha'Agur, but the Arizal followed it only in a tallit katan, not in a large tallit. His son Rabbi Shmuel Vital testified that his father, Rabbi Chaim Vital, did not follow it even in a tallit katan. It seems that Rabbi Chaim Vital understood from his teacher the Arizal that this matter is not indispensable, and that the Arizal continued with it only because he had been accustomed to it in his childhood, following the custom of the Ashkenazim - and so Rabbi Chaim Vital likewise did not change his own personal custom. The Ben Ish Chai notes that the accepted custom today, even among the Chassidim of Jerusalem, is to make only a single hole in each corner, whether in a large tallit or a small tallit, and this was presumably also the custom of the Rashash.
takeaways: There were different approaches among the students of the Arizal regarding the number of holes in the corner (one or two), but this does not affect the basic validity of the mitzvah.
The accepted custom today, including in Jerusalem, is to make only a single hole in each corner - both in a large tallit and a small tallit.

paragraphs: It is not proper to leave the tallit unfolded at night, and if one forgot and did not fold it and the night passed over it, then when he wears it the next day he should first shake it out, as mentioned by the later authorities. It is also written by the later authorities that everyone should fold his own tallit himself, by hand, every day after prayer, and not give it to the sexton to fold, since that is harmful to one's fortune. One should also take care, when removing the tallit and likewise the tefillin, to remove them with the left hand, which is the weaker hand, to show that parting from them is difficult for him.

clarification.explanation: It is not proper to leave the tallit unfolded overnight - one should fold it every day. If one forgot and did not fold it and the night passed, he should only wear it the next day after first shaking it out, as the later authorities wrote. The later authorities also wrote that everyone should fold his own tallit by hand, immediately after prayer, and not hand it to the sexton to fold, since that is harmful to one's fortune. Likewise, when removing the tallit and the tefillin, one should remove them with the left hand (the weaker, less prominent hand), to show that the parting from the mitzvah is difficult for him.
takeaways: One should fold his own tallit (not have someone else do it) immediately after prayer; and if he forgot and it was left unfolded overnight, he should shake it out before wearing it the next day.
One should remove the tallit and tefillin specifically with the left hand, as an expression that the parting from the mitzvah is difficult.

paragraphs: It is proper to look at the tzitzit, and to intend and picture in one's mind as if there were among them a thread of the appearance of techelet, resembling the sky, since that illumination has never ceased, as our teacher Rabbi Chaim Vital of blessed memory wrote, and one will find it good to have this intention.

clarification.explanation: It is proper to look at the tzitzit, and to intend and imagine in one's mind as though there were among them a thread of techelet color, resembling the color of the sky - for even though we do not have actual techelet in our time, its illumination has, in truth, never ceased, as Rabbi Chaim Vital wrote. One who directs this intention while looking at the tzitzit will find great spiritual benefit in it.
takeaways: Even without actual techelet, it is recommended to look at the tzitzit and imagine within them a thread of techelet the color of the sky, since the spiritual illumination of techelet has never ceased.
